title: Natural enemy interactions constrain pest control in complex agricultural landscapes
authors: Martin EA, Reineking B, Seo B, Steffan-Dewenter I
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
location: Haean, South Korea (128°5' to 128°11' E, 38°13' to 38°20' N)
design: Field exclusion experiment in 18 fields across a 55-km² agricultural landscape; 6 natural enemy exclusion treatments per field plus 1 abiotic control: -B (birds excluded, chicken wire 1.5 cm mesh), -G (ground-dwellers excluded, plastic sheets + insect glue + pitfall traps), -F-B (flying insects + birds excluded, polyester mesh 0.8 mm + chicken wire), -G-B (ground-dwellers + birds excluded), -G-F-B (all enemies excluded), O (open, no exclusion); exclusion cages 50 × 150 × 100 cm with 20 m² plots; 4 cabbage plants per treatment per plot; initial pest densities standardized across exclosures; 60-day growth period (July-September 2010); (G)LMM with treatment × landscape complexity interaction; n = 318 for pest density (cage-level counts across rounds), n = 432 for herbivory and biomass (plant-level measurements)
notes: This paper's central finding is that natural enemy INTERACTIONS (particularly antagonistic intraguild predation by birds on flying insect predators) constrain pest control in complex landscapes. In simple landscapes, all enemy guilds contribute positively. In complex landscapes, birds reduce the effectiveness of flying insect predators through intraguild predation. This means the direction of the bird-exclusion effect depends on landscape complexity — averaged across all landscapes, -B vs O may be non-significant because opposite effects cancel out. The paper reports three response variables: pest larval density (Lepidoptera larvae per cage), herbivory (% leaf damage), and fresh biomass (g per plant). All three are measured at the end of the 60-day growth period. The overall effect of all enemy guilds combined (-G-F-B vs O) is stated in text: 43% lower pest density, 54% lower leaf damage, and 57% higher biomass for O relative to -G-F-B. These percentages are from model predictions (backtransformed, accounting for estimation uncertainty). Figure 1 shows raw means ± SEM per treatment. The bar ordering in Figure 1 corresponds to the 6 treatments shown with icon symbols indicating which guilds are excluded. Table 2 gives pairwise treatment comparisons for herbivory (slope and intercept differences). For the -B vs O comparison specifically: slope difference = 0.014, P(adjusted) = 0.254 (NS); intercept difference = -0.169, P(adjusted) = 0.813 (NS) — confirming no significant overall effect of bird exclusion alone on herbivory. Pest density was modeled with negative binomial, herbivory was logit-transformed, biomass modeled with Gamma distribution. Landscape complexity measured as % seminatural habitat at 300 m radius (AIC-selected scale).

figure_read.structure: Panel C of three-panel figure. Six bars representing 6 exclusion treatments, each with mean ± SEM. Y-axis: Biomass (g), fresh biomass of individual plants. Ticks at 0, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250; spacing 50 g; linear. Error bars are SEM (caption: 'means ± SEM per treatment'). Tukey letters above bars (adjusted P < 0.05). Treatment identity shown by small guild icons below each bar — crossed-out symbols indicate excluded guilds (wasp = flying insects, beetle = ground-dwellers, bird = birds/vertebrates). The O (open) bar appears tallest; the bar with letter 'b' appears shortest.
figure_read.evidence_note: Figure has 6 bars with small guild-icon labels that are difficult to resolve at available PDF resolution. Cannot reliably match specific bars to specific treatments from the icon symbols alone. However, the text states O has 57% higher biomass than -G-F-B, which constrains the values. The tallest bar (O) reads approximately 185-195 g; -G-F-B should then be approximately 118-124 g (185-195 / 1.57). One bar with Tukey letter 'b' appears at approximately 80-100 g — this is likely NOT -G-F-B but rather a partial exclusion treatment affected by antagonistic interactions. Absolute means not reported in text.

observations.notes: Text states: 'treatments accessible to all natural enemies led to... 57% higher biomass than controls excluding enemies.' This means O biomass = 1.57 × -G-F-B biomass. The effect_pct is calculated as: 100 × (1/1.57 - 1) = -36.3% (the -G-F-B treatment has 36.3% less biomass than O). Absolute means not stated in text. Figure 1C shows raw means ± SEM but the 6-bar figure with icon-based treatment labels cannot be reliably digitized at this PDF resolution — the specific bars for O and -G-F-B cannot be confidently identified. The 57% figure is from model predictions (backtransformed) per the Methods.

figure_read.evidence_note: Same limitation — 6 bars with icon labels. Text states O has 43% lower pest density than -G-F-B. One bar has Tukey letter 'd' (significantly different from all others, highest) — likely -G-F-B. Another has letter 'b' (low) — could be O or -B. Pest density modeled with negative binomial. Specific bar heights: the 'd' bar appears at approximately 5-7 larvae/cage; the 'b' bar at approximately 1-3 larvae/cage.

observations.notes: Text states: 'treatments accessible to all natural enemies led to 43% lower pest densities... than controls excluding enemies.' So -G-F-B has 1/(1-0.43) = 1.754× the pest density of O. effect_pct = +75.4%. Pest density = total number of Lepidoptera larvae (Pieris rapae, P. brassicae, Trichoplusia ni) per exclusion cage. Modeled with negative binomial distribution. P < 0.001 for treatment effect (Table 1). In complex landscapes, densities reached ~11 larvae/exclosure vs ~1 in simple landscapes. Direction: excluding all enemies increases pest abundance as expected.

The -B bar likely shares Tukey letter 'ab' with O ('a'), indicating no significant difference. Table 2 confirms -B vs O herbivory intercept is non-significant (P adjusted = 0.813). Biomass comparison not separately reported in text.

observations.notes: Bird-only exclusion (-B) vs open control (O). No specific percentage or mean difference stated in text for this comparison. Table 2 shows -B vs O is NOT significant for herbivory (slope P adj = 0.254, intercept P adj = 0.813). The paper's key finding is that bird effects are landscape-dependent: in simple landscapes, birds contribute positively to pest control; in complex landscapes, birds constrain flying insect predators through intraguild predation. Averaged across all 18 landscapes, the -B vs O comparison is non-significant. Figure 1 bars for -B and O appear similar but cannot be reliably digitized due to 6-bar density and icon-based labels.

observations.notes: Bird-only exclusion vs open is NOT significant for herbivory. Table 2 pairwise comparison: -B vs O slope P(adjusted) = 0.254, intercept P(adjusted) = 0.813. The non-significance is because bird effects are landscape-dependent: in simple landscapes birds reduce herbivory, in complex landscapes birds constrain flying insect predators (intraguild predation) which can paradoxically increase herbivory. These opposite effects cancel out across the landscape gradient.

figure_read.evidence_note: Cannot identify specific -B bar. In simple landscapes, excluding birds (-B) increases pest density (reduced biocontrol). In complex landscapes, excluding birds decreases pest density (released flying insect predators from intraguild predation). Averaged effect likely non-significant.

observations.notes: Bird-only exclusion vs open for pest density. No specific comparison stated in text. The paper reports that 'densities... showing lower densities and damage in treatments excluding birds, than in those including them (Fig. 1 A and B)', which suggests that AVERAGED across landscapes, -B may actually have LOWER pest density than O. This is the opposite of the simple biocontrol expectation and is the paper's key finding: birds can constrain pest control through intraguild predation. Direction check: if -B < O for pest density, this means excluding birds REDUCES pests — opposite to expected. This is a real finding, not a treatment/control swap. The paper explicitly discusses this as antagonistic natural enemy interactions. Re-checked assignment: -B is the bird-excluded arm (treatment), O is the open arm (control). The negative direction (excluding birds reduces pests) is correct for this system where birds suppress flying insect predators.
